lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I should be seated ahead of you, Libyan. I am better.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: You absolutely shouldn't. I am.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Let Minos decide, then.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: [Sighs] And who are you?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: This is Hannibal the Carthaginian, and I am Alexander, son of Philip.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Famous names, both of you. What are you arguing about?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Seating arrangements. He claims he was a better general than me. And I maintain—as the entire world knows—that I was vastly superior not just to him, but to almost everyone who has ever waged war.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Make your cases one at a time. You first, the Libyan. Go.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: Well, Minos, I’ve had the benefit of picking up fluent Greek down here, so he can't even claim an advantage over me there. My argument is this: true greatness belongs to the men who start with nothing and forge their own power. I went to Spain with a handful of men, starting as a mere subordinate to my brother. I rose to supreme command because I was the best. I conquered the Celtiberians. I crushed the western Gauls. I crossed the Alps, overran the entire Po valley, sacked city after city, brought the Italian plains to their knees, and marched right up to the suburbs of Rome itself. I killed so many men in a single day that we measured their gold rings by the bushel and used their corpses to bridge rivers.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: And I did all of this without calling myself the son of Ammon, or pretending to be a god, or broadcasting my mother’s prophetic dreams. I was a mortal man. I fought the smartest generals in the world. I engaged the most formidable soldiers. I didn't just chase after Medes and Armenians who run away before anyone even attacks them and hand victory to anyone with the nerve to show up.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: Alexander, on the other hand, inherited his father’s empire. He expanded it, yes, but mostly by riding a massive wave of luck. And the moment he won—the moment he beat that pathetic coward Darius at Issus and Arbela—he abandoned his ancestral customs, demanded people worship him, started dressing up like a Persian, and made a habit of murdering his own friends at dinner parties.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: I treated my country as an equal. When a massive enemy fleet sailed against Carthage and I was recalled, I went back immediately. I laid down my command, stepped back into private life, and when they exiled me, I took it with good grace. And I did all this as a 'barbarian.' No Greek education. No quoting Homer. No private tutoring from that sophist Aristotle. Just natural ability.

lines.speaker: Hannibal
lines.text: That is why I say I am better than Alexander. If he looks prettier because he tied a ribbon around his head—well, maybe Macedonians care about that sort of thing. But it doesn't make him a better man than a commander who relied on his brain rather than his luck.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: Well. That was a rather decent speech. Unusually articulate for a Libyan. What do you have to say to that, Alexander?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I really shouldn't have to dignify such staggering arrogance with a response, Minos. Global reputation alone should tell you the difference between the king I was and the bandit he was. But let's just see if my achievements are 'lucky.'

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I took the throne as a mere boy. The kingdom was in chaos. I tracked down my father's assassins. I terrified Greece into submission by flattening Thebes. They elected me Supreme Commander, but I wasn't about to sit around Macedonia happily ruling what my father left me. I looked at the whole world, and decided it would be a disgrace not to own it. I invaded Asia with a fraction of his numbers. I won a massive victory at the Granicus. I took Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia—rolling over everything in my path—until I reached Issus, where Darius was waiting with an army of hundreds of thousands.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: And you know what happened next, Minos. You know exactly how many dead men I sent down to you in a single day. The ferryman still complains about it—he said his boat couldn't handle the volume, they had to build rafts to get across! And I did this leading from the front, taking wounds myself.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I won't even bore you with Tyre or Arbela. I marched all the way to India. I made the Ocean the border of my empire. I captured their elephants. I crushed King Porus. I crossed the Don and routed the Scythians—who are not exactly pushovers—in a massive cavalry battle. I rewarded my friends and annihilated my enemies. And if people thought I was a god, well, considering the sheer scale of what I was doing, you can hardly blame them for believing it!

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: And lastly: I died a king. He died in exile, groveling at the court of Prusias of Bithynia—exactly the death a vicious, treacherous thug deserves. Because let's be honest about how he conquered the Italians: not by force of arms, but by deceit, treachery, and cheap tricks. Nothing lawful, nothing face-to-face. And since he brings up my 'luxury,' he seems to have conveniently forgotten his little winter in Capua, where this great military genius spent the crucial phase of the war lounging around with prostitutes!

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: If I hadn't considered the West too trivial to bother with and turned East instead, would taking Italy without a fight really have been such a massive achievement? Or Africa? Or the Straits of Gibraltar? They were already cowering. They already recognized their master. I rest my case. Judge us, Minos. There's plenty more I could say, but that's enough.

lines.speaker: Scipio
lines.text: [Stepping forward] Don't rule until you've heard from me.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: And who exactly are you, my good man? Where are you speaking from?

lines.speaker: Scipio
lines.text: Scipio of Italy. The general who leveled Carthage and conquered the Libyans in battle.

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: And what is your point?

lines.speaker: Scipio
lines.text: That I am inferior to Alexander. But I am superior to Hannibal. I defeated him. I chased him down and forced him into a disgraceful retreat.

lines.speaker: Scipio
lines.text: So how incredibly shameless is this man, competing for first place against Alexander—a man that even I, the man who beat Hannibal, wouldn't presume to compare myself to?

lines.speaker: Minos
lines.text: [Chuckles] A very elegant argument, Scipio. Well then. Alexander is ranked first. You are second. And Hannibal—who is, let's be fair, not entirely insignificant—can take third. Next case!
